explanations.explanation: Jesus tells him, “If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” That's the whole answer, and it fits on one line, which is more than I can say for my recipe cards. He says it right after telling the man, “There is only One who is good.” (Matthew 19:17)

Feasts is a fun guess, and my ovens would vote for it. But Jesus doesn't mention a single feast in this passage. He says, “If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” Then the man asks which ones, and Jesus starts naming them.

Traditions sound like a safe bet, since every family has that one way of doing things. Jesus doesn't use that word here, though. He says, “If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” The man's very next question is about which commandments, so that word stays at the center.

Jesus finishes the list with “…and love your neighbor as yourself.” Say it with me: even the neighbor whose leaf blower fires up at 7 a.m. Jesus doesn't add that part, that's just my street talking. The list that started with “Do not murder” lands right on loving your neighbor.

The Sabbath is a real commandment, so your memory is working fine (Exodus 20:8). But it isn't on the list Jesus gives this man. His list in Matthew 19:18-19 ends with “…and love your neighbor as yourself.” Keep that one in your back pocket, though.

That one is in the Ten Commandments, so you're digging in the right drawer (Exodus 20:4). Jesus just doesn't read it to this man. His list stops with honor your father and mother, and then He adds, “…and love your neighbor as yourself.” Sometimes the answer is hiding at the end of the list.

The young man says, “All these I have kept.” That is a man with confidence. I once told my oven timer I'd never scorch another batch, and the timer just stayed quiet. Then he asks Jesus another question, and that's where the story really starts moving.
The man doesn't say he missed any of them. He says, “All these I have kept.” He's looking at the whole list and answering yes. Then he asks Jesus one more question, which is the interesting part.

He asks, “What do I still lack?” I think that's a man who has checked every box and still feels a little draft in the room. That's an honest thing to ask out loud. And Jesus gives him a direct answer.

That question does get asked in Matthew, but by someone else, in a different scene. An expert in the law asks Jesus which commandment is the greatest (Matthew 22:35-36). Here the young man asks, “What do I still lack?” Same neighborhood, different conversation.
That question is in the Bible too, just not here. An expert in the law asks it in Luke 10:25, 29. This young man asks, “What do I still lack?” Keep a bookmark in Luke for that other one.

Jesus says, “…and you will have treasure in heaven.” Notice He doesn't just say what to let go of, He says what comes next. Then He adds, “Then come, follow Me.” For the record, my own treasure is a gold base and a mustache, and I'm doing fine.

A seat in the temple sounds nice and comfy, but Jesus doesn't promise that here. He says, “…and you will have treasure in heaven.” The promise comes with an invitation to follow Him. No temple seating chart anywhere in the verse.

Honor in Jerusalem is a big promise, and Jesus doesn't make it in this passage. What He says is, “…and you will have treasure in heaven.” Then He tells the man to come and follow Him. Jerusalem doesn't even come up.
Jesus says, “Then come, follow Me.” That's the invitation sitting right at the end of the instruction. It isn't only about what gets sold. It's also about who he'd be walking with.
Praise is a good thing to do, and I do plenty of it over my cookie dough. But the word Jesus uses here is different. He says, “Then come, follow Me.” It's an invitation to walk alongside Him.
Thank is a kind word, and it's a close neighbor to the right one. But Jesus doesn't say thank here. He says, “Then come, follow Me.” The invitation is to go with Him.

The text says the young man “went away in sorrow.” I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story. He came running with a big question and left with a heavy heart. I'm not going to joke about that one.
The passage doesn't say anger. It says he “went away in sorrow.” I think that's a quieter, heavier thing than being mad. Sometimes a person leaves a room sad, not slamming the door.

I'd love to tell you he left skipping, but that's not what the text says. It says he “went away in sorrow.” I think this is a sad moment in the story, so I'll just say it plainly. His sorrow is part of what the passage records.

The passage says he went away in sorrow “because he had great wealth.” That's the reason the text gives, and it doesn't add any others. Jesus had just told him to sell his possessions and give to the poor. I think that's a lot to hold in two hands.

That's a reasonable guess, but the text doesn't say it. It gives one reason: “because he had great wealth.” No family emergency is mentioned anywhere in these verses. When the passage gives the reason, I'll stick with the reason it gives.

Religious leaders don't appear in this scene at all. The text gives one reason for his leaving: “because he had great wealth.” I won't add one the passage doesn't state. The reason is already sitting right there in the verse.

The text says, “they were greatly astonished.” Greatly, not a little. I picture a whole group going quiet at the same time, like someone just announced the oven's been off all day. Then they ask Him a question.
They do react, and it's a big one. The text says, “they were greatly astonished.” That's a group of people who did not expect to hear what they just heard. After that they ask Jesus a question.

They ask, “Who then can be saved?” That's what a group of astonished people says when the ground just moved. I think they're asking it out loud because everyone's thinking it. And Jesus looks right at them to answer.

Good question, but it's not the one they ask. The text says they ask, “Who then can be saved?” Giving up everything comes up later, when Peter says they have left everything to follow Jesus. That's a different moment.

explanations.answer: Is it wrong to have wealth
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful question, but the disciples don't ask it here. What they ask is, “Who then can be saved?” They're astonished, and that's the question that comes out. Jesus answers that one.

explanations.answer: With God all things are possible
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” He's answering a question about who can be saved. It puts all the weight on God, not on us. That's good news for anybody who has ever burned the first tray.

explanations.answer: With God the rich must give more
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that to His disciples here. He says, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” The second half is the one to hold onto. It points at what God can do, not at a bigger bill.

explanations.answer: With God only the poor get in
explanations.explanation: That isn't what Jesus says. He tells the disciples, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Notice the word all. He doesn't draw a line around who gets included in that.

explanations.answer: Judge the twelve tribes of Israel
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the disciples “will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” That's quite the promotion for a group that just heard a camel and a needle in the same sentence. He says it will happen in the renewal of all things. Twelve thrones is a big seating chart.

explanations.answer: Build the new city of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Building isn't what Jesus mentions here. He says they “will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” No hard hats, no blueprints. Just thrones and a job on them.

Singing and angels don't come up in these verses. Jesus says they “will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Their job there is judging. I'll keep my humming for the oven.

Jesus says everyone who has left those things for His name “will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.” The hundredfold is big, and eternal life comes right alongside it. It's the same eternal life the young man asked about at the start. The story comes back around to it.

Earthly is a fair guess after hearing about houses and fields. But the text says they “will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.” The life Jesus names is eternal. It's the very thing the young man asked about in verse 16.

Peaceful sounds lovely, like a quiet kitchen after the last batch cools. But that isn't the word Jesus uses. He says they “will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.” Eternal is the word, and it matches the young man's first question.

Jesus actually says, “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.” The second half turns around instead of staying put. So the last do not stay last. That little flip is the part to remember.

Right, the second half is different. Jesus says, “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.” The last don't stay last, they end up first. I'd say that's the part worth underlining.
